summary: Defines a human-readable string form for LDAP search filters, which travel on the wire in a binary form. The string form suits LDAP URLs and other applications. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A way to write search rules in plain text, like find everyone named Sam in this city.

subtitle: How to write an LDAP search filter as readable text, such as (&(objectClass=Person)(sn=Jensen)).

tldr.problem: LDAP search filters travel over the network in a binary form that people and applications cannot easily read, write or embed in places like LDAP URLs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an ABNF grammar for a prefix-notation text form in which every filter sits in parentheses, with &, | and ! for and, or and not, and a backslash-plus-two-hex-digits escape for special octets.
tldr.outcome: Applications get one common, UTF-8 based way to write any LDAP version 3 filter, including extended match filters. It replaces RFC 2254.

today: RFC 4515 is a Proposed Standard. It obsoletes RFC 2254 and, according to the unit metadata, has not itself been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why a String Form of Filters
sections.content:
The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) sends a search filter to a server as a binary structure. RFC 4515 defines a human-readable string format for that same filter, so applications can show, store or exchange it as text. LDAP URLs (RFC 4516) are named as one such application.

The string format covers the full range of LDAP version 3 search filters, including extended match filters. The document is part of the LDAP technical specification (RFC 4510) and replaces RFC 2254.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers normally pass search questions around in a secret code. This note gives a way to write the same question in words and symbols that a person can read.

sections.title: The Binary Filter Being Represented
sections.content:
Section 2 repeats the filter definition from RFC 4511 in ASN.1. A Filter is a choice of ten forms: and, or, not, equalityMatch, substrings, greaterOrEqual, lessOrEqual, present, approxMatch and extensibleMatch.

Most comparisons pair an attribute description with an assertion value. A substring filter holds an optional initial part, any number of any parts and an optional final part; initial and final can occur at most once. An extensible match can name a matching rule, an attribute type and a dnAttributes flag that defaults to false.

On the wire the filter is encoded with the Basic Encoding Rules (BER), with simplifications described in RFC 4511.
sections.plainLanguage: A filter is built from a few kinds of building blocks: and, or, not, equals, bigger, smaller, has-a-value and sounds-like. The text form needs a way to write each block.

sections.title: The String Grammar
sections.content:
A filter string is UTF-8 text defined by an ABNF grammar and uses prefix notation: the operator comes first. Every filter is wrapped in parentheses. Three operators combine filters: & for and, | for or, and ! for not. And and or take a list of one or more filters; not takes exactly one.

The simple comparisons are written as follows.

  • = for equality
  • ~= for approximate match
  • >= for greater or equal
  • <= for less or equal

A presence test is attr=*. A substring test puts asterisks where the unknown text goes, for example (o=univ*of*mich*). Although the grammar can produce attr=* as both a substring and a presence filter, it is used only to denote presence.

An extensible match has the shape attr:dn:matchingrule:=value, where the attribute, the :dn flag and the :oid matching rule are each optional, but at least the attribute or the matching rule must be present.
sections.plainLanguage: You put each rule in brackets and write the joining word first, like (and rule1 rule2). A star means anything can go here, and special signs mean equals, bigger or smaller.

sections.title: Escaping Special Characters
sections.content:
The valueencoding rule makes sure the whole filter is valid UTF-8 and removes parsing ambiguity. The octets for the asterisk (0x2a), left parenthesis (0x28), right parenthesis (0x29), backslash (0x5c) and NUL (0x00) must be written as a backslash followed by two hexadecimal digits. So a filter for a cn value containing an asterisk anywhere is written with \2a between two substring markers. Other octets in the normal set may be escaped the same way, for example non-printing ASCII characters.

For a non-ASCII character, each UTF-8 octet is escaped separately. This escaping lets any filter that LDAP can represent be written as a NUL-terminated string.

Implementations MUST escape all octets greater than 0x7F that are not part of a valid UTF-8 sequence when they generate a filter string. They SHOULD accept input that is not valid UTF-8, because RFC 2254 never clearly said that the string form was UTF-8 text.
sections.plainLanguage: Some characters, like brackets and stars, already mean something in a filter. To use them as plain letters you write a backslash and a short code instead, like putting quote marks around a word.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives several filters. (&(objectClass=Person)(|(sn=Jensen)(cn=Babs J*))) matches entries of class Person whose surname is Jensen or whose common name starts with Babs J. (!(cn=Tim Howes)) excludes one name, and (seeAlso=) is an equality test against an empty value.

For extensible matching, (cn:caseExactMatch:=Fred Flintstone) names a matching rule, while (cn:=Betty Rubble) omits it. In (sn:dn:2.4.6.8.10:=Barney Rubble) the OID picks the rule and :dn means the parts of the entry's distinguished name count as part of the entry. If the attribute is left out, as in (:1.2.3:=Wilma Flintstone), the filter applies to any attribute that supports that rule. The dn flag is case insensitive, as (:DN:2.4.6.8.10:=Dino) shows.

Escaping examples include (o=Parens R Us \28for all your parenthetical needs\29), (filename=C:\5cMyFile), (bin=\00\00\00\04) for four arbitrary octets, and (sn=Lu\c4\8di\c4\87) for the five characters of a name with non-ASCII letters.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show real searches, such as everyone whose name is Jensen, or everyone whose name is not Tim. They also show how to write a star or a bracket when you mean the actual character.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the string representation itself has no known security implications. LDAP search filters do, because servers interpret them to select the entries from which data is retrieved. Servers should take care to protect the data they hold from unauthorized access.

It points readers to the security sections of RFC 4511 and RFC 4513 for more.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing a question in words is harmless. What matters is that the server only answers questions from people who are allowed to see the answers.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 2254
sections.content:
Appendix A lists the differences from RFC 2254. The main technical changes are these.

  • The string is now stated to be UTF-8 encoded Unicode.
  • The ABNF reuses common productions from RFC 4512.
  • The value rule became assertionvalue, matching RFC 4517.
  • The greater and less rules became greaterorequal and lessorequal to avoid confusion.
  • New valueencoding, normal and escaped rules reduce dependence on descriptive text.

The examples section also gained four new examples, and the references were reorganised.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a cleaned-up version of an older note. The rules are written more carefully, and the names are clearer, so nobody mixes up bigger and smaller.

items.label: and
items.desc: Matches when every filter in the list matches.

items.label: or
items.desc: Matches when any filter in the list matches.

items.label: extensible
items.desc: Extensible match, with optional :dn and :oid parts.
